title: Hyperscalers and sovereign AI
lede: When the four largest American hyperscalers collectively pledged roughly $690 billion in capital expenditure for 2026, the conventional read was euphoria for AI chipmakers. Serenity's read was more specific: the headline numbers were a demand signal for the upstream supply chains she had quietly been accumulating since mid-2025, not a reason to buy the hyperscalers themselves.
body:
When Alphabet (GOOGL), Microsoft (MSFT), Meta Platforms (META), and Amazon.com (AMZN) reported their spring 2026 earnings, the capital-expenditure figures were extraordinary even by the standards of the AI buildout. Meta's full-year 2025 capex reached $72 billion; the company then raised its 2026 guidance to $125–145 billion. Microsoft guided for quarterly capex above $40 billion in the June quarter, implying a calendar-year run-rate near $190 billion. Alphabet logged $91 billion for 2025 and guided to roughly $175 billion for 2026. Amazon's 2025 capital spending topped $128 billion, with 2026 commitments exceeding $200 billion. Combined, the four companies had pledged around $690 billion in a single calendar year to building the infrastructure of artificial intelligence.

Serenity watched those earnings calls closely—and drew a different conclusion from them than most observers.

> I've monitored the situation for you. TLDR on hyperscaler capex spend (signal aside from $TSM). From $MSFT, $AMZN, $META earnings: Upstream semi supply chains go brrr. $META: 2026 FY capex $115–$135B, Revised Q1 ER: $125B–$145B capex raised. -> Higher component prices

The key phrase is “signal aside from $TSM.” For Serenity, hyperscaler earnings calls are not investment theses in themselves but primary data releases confirming demand for the upstream supply chains they actually own. The hyperscalers are the demand signal; the trade is in the components.

## NVIDIA and the custom-silicon challenge

This framing explains a paradox in Serenity’s public record. Nvidia (NVDA) dominates the AI accelerator market—its Blackwell GPU families are the *de facto* standard for AI training at every major hyperscaler, and its *CUDA* software ecosystem creates switching costs that competing hardware has struggled to overcome. Nvidia logged $186 billion in data-centre revenue for its fiscal year ending January 2026, up 65% year-on-year, on a forward P/E of roughly 17.5 times. Yet Serenity’s measured alpha on NVDA is a modest 0.12, well below their signal on Marvell Technology (MRVL) at 1.07.

The explanation is partly valuation—much of the obvious good news already priced in—and partly their reading of the custom-silicon shift. They named the tension explicitly in late 2025: “I can argue the bear case for $NVDA too, that hyperscalers are building their own ASICs. But in cases like these, you look at numbers rather than narrative—the backlog for Nvidia is wild.” Their resolution was to hold both: Nvidia for its installed base and CUDA lock-in, while accumulating separately the companies building the alternative trajectory.

By 2026 that alternative was fully operational. Broadcom (AVGO) was building *tensor processing units* (TPUs) for Alphabet (GOOGL) under a supply agreement extending to 2031, while simultaneously developing Meta Platforms’ (META) proprietary training chips; its first-quarter AI revenue hit $8.4 billion, up 106% year-on-year. Marvell was developing *XPUs*—custom AI accelerators—for at least three major hyperscaler customers, with a $75 billion lifetime-revenue pipeline disclosed at its 2025 investor event. Broadcom’s CEO Hock Tan has guided to $60–90 billion in AI chip revenue by 2027 from three hyperscaler customers alone. Serenity’s summary of Broadcom’s role required just four words: “Long hyperscaler ASIC.”

## Marvell: the hidden hyperscaler play

Of the two custom-silicon names, Marvell Technology (MRVL) has been Serenity’s highest-conviction call in this cluster. Their entry came in early September 2025, when the stock fell 18% following an earnings miss the market briefly treated as fundamental deterioration.

> $MRVL 18% drop after earnings was a complete overreaction. Perfect time to DCA into Marvell positions over the next month.

Marvell’s eventual FY2026 result—record revenue of $8.2 billion, up 42%, with data-centre sales reaching 74% of total—bore them out. The specific driver they tracked was Microsoft’s (MSFT) Maia custom AI accelerator, a chip built on Marvell silicon under a long-term programme. By April 2026 they had added a second hyperscaler to the thesis: “I liked $MRVL back at $80 and even here, mainly because of $MSFT Maia. But having $GOOGL as a likely customer for revenue visibility past 2028 helps a lot too. They’re really milking that Celestial acquisition.” Marvell’s Celestial division—acquired in 2021 for its custom silicon expertise—is the technical engine behind its hyperscaler XPU programmes.

Their characterisation of the broader opportunity captures its market-structure logic precisely:

> I feel like $COHR and $MRVL are the two “They Do Everything” longs. That nobody actually knows what they do if you ask them in public. $NVDA? GPUs. $INTC? Foundry. Marvell? No clue. Coherent? No clue. They’re the Deloitte of Semis.

Breadth of exposure, low retail awareness, institutional reluctance to underwrite complex stories before revenue appears: the information arbitrage is the alpha. Marvell spans optical DSPs for coherent networking, Ethernet *SerDes* components, enterprise storage controllers, and the XPU programmes that tie directly to two confirmed hyperscaler customers—with a third reportedly in development. Sell-side consensus had not fully modelled the Maia ramp when Serenity began building their position at $80.

## ARM and the CPU bottleneck

An original angle in Serenity’s framework concerns ARM Holdings (ARM). They took a position in late March 2026 when the company released new AI CPU roadmap news, framing ARM as a potential “NVDA for CPUs.” By late April they had a specific bottleneck thesis in view: Intel’s chief executive had disclosed that AI inference was pushing the CPU-to-GPU ratio from 1:8 toward 1:1, implying a structural step-up in CPU demand. “Bullish on $ARM, given the new bottleneck shifting back to CPUs,” they wrote. “I’m predicting parts of localised inference to be handled by CPUs more and more… as models like Gemma get lightweight in the future.”

The thesis has structural support: ARM’s Neoverse architecture already underpins the majority of hyperscaler custom CPU cores—AWS Graviton, Google Axion, Microsoft Cobalt—and Arm projects that Arm-based designs could account for roughly 90% of host CPU deployments in custom AI ASIC servers by 2029, up from around 25% in 2025. At a forward P/E near 99 times, the valuation case is thin, and Serenity acknowledges it; they hold ARM as an option on an architecture cycle, not a value entry.

## Discounts and derivatives

Microsoft (MSFT) they approached as a contrarian entry. Spotting the stock near $372 in March 2026—briefly trading through its 200-week moving average for the first time in thirteen years, roughly 33% below its July 2025 all-time high—they went long, noting it looked “too discounted.” The logic was straightforward: a business generating $37 billion in annualised AI revenue with Azure growing 40% year-on-year warranted a better multiple than the market briefly assigned.

For *high-bandwidth memory* (HBM) exposure they turned to the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), buying 2028 leaps as a vehicle for Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix without navigating Korean market access directly.

> I’m still personally long 2028 leaps on $EWY for memory exposure. Those are up over triple digits, since I expect Samsung/SK Hynix to be printing.

EWY recovered sharply from February 2026 lows that had prompted widespread “KOSPI crash bubble” commentary, validating a thesis that is at bottom simple: *HBM* demand cannot exist without the Korean memory duopoly. The trade also illustrates their preference for proxies—capturing a structural bottleneck through the most liquid available vehicle rather than navigating illiquid foreign-listed names directly. Korean-listed HBM suppliers became accessible to them via IBKR only in late April 2026, at which point they began researching direct positions.

On the broader sovereign AI buildout—Nvidia’s (NVDA) agreement with Saudi Arabia’s HUMAIN to deploy hundreds of thousands of Blackwell GPUs, the European Investment Bank’s €70 billion technology commitment, India’s national compute initiative—Serenity has been largely silent as a theme. Oracle (ORCL), whose Stargate joint venture with OpenAI and SoftBank carries a $523 billion remaining-performance-obligation backlog, appears in their September 2025 watchlists but not as a primary thesis. Their reasoning is structural rather than geopolitical: sovereign capex ultimately flows through the same *CoWoS* advanced-packaging bottleneck at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM), the same EUV lithography machines from ASML Holding (ASML), and the same photonics and networking components they have catalogued since mid-2025. The map changes; the chokepoints do not.

concepts.definition: Compute Unified Device Architecture: Nvidia’s proprietary parallel-computing platform and programming model. Because virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, switching to non-Nvidia accelerators requires substantial engineering investment, creating deep customer lock-in.

A chip designed from scratch for a specific hyperscaler’s AI workloads, as opposed to a commodity GPU. Google’s TPU, Microsoft’s Maia, and Amazon’s Trainium are all XPUs. Marvell designs and manufactures XPUs for hyperscalers under long-term supply agreements.

TSMC’s advanced packaging technology that stacks logic chips and high-bandwidth memory onto a shared silicon interposer, enabling the dense GPU-plus-HBM configurations used in AI accelerators. Capacity is tightly constrained and allocated years in advance.

Stacked DRAM designed for extreme memory bandwidth rather than density. Nvidia’s H100 and H200 GPUs each carry up to 80–141 GB of HBM3/HBM3e, manufactured almost exclusively by SK Hynix and Samsung. HBM is a critical bottleneck in AI accelerator supply chains.

Semiconductor IP that converts parallel data streams to high-speed serial links for chip-to-chip and chip-to-optic interconnects inside data centres. Marvell is a leading supplier of high-speed SerDes for AI networking.

Chipmaking process that uses 13.5-nanometre light to print the finest circuit features on leading-edge semiconductors. ASML is the sole manufacturer of EUV machines; every advanced AI chip depends on them.
